items.text: Simultaneously distinguishing explicit common‑cause judgments and modality‑specific perceptual shifts across the full horizontal plane can reveal the distinct ranges of unity and influence, rather than measuring only fusion weights.
Two adaptation paradigms, modality‑specific measurements, and generalization beyond training can differentiate local learning from more general perceptual recalibration.

Longitudinal observation of acute injury and correction of chronic shifts connect pathological mechanisms to future rehabilitation; the perceptual retention results of this project are valuable in themselves and are not equivalent to a functional efficacy trial.

Binary unity judgments and continuous directional shifts are susceptible to task, response criterion, and directional bias effects; measurement separation alone is insufficient to uniquely determine a common‑cause computational model and requires explicit comparative interpretation.

Chronic adaptation lacks a concurrent sham‑adaptation control, arranges the two methods by enrollment order, and enrolls participants with larger baseline shifts—introducing regression to the mean, order effects, and cross‑session carryover; shift improvement does not directly demonstrate symptomatic efficacy.

Approximately 30 patients must accommodate 16 acute cases with ~50% dropout, at least 20 chronic cases, and multi‑etiology subgroups—recruitment capacity and inferential precision are mismatched; multiple condition repetitions further increase burden and multiple comparisons.
